As Large Language Models (LLMs) become increasingly popular, developers are discovering that models like GPT, Claude, and Gemini cannot inherently remember private documents, company knowledge bases, or real-time information.
This is where vector databases come into the picture.
One of the most popular vector databases among AI developers is Chroma. Designed specifically for AI applications, Chroma makes it easy to store, search, and retrieve embeddings that power modern Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems.
In this article, we’ll explore what Chroma is, how it works, and why it’s widely used in AI applications.
The Problem Chroma Solves
Imagine you have thousands of documents:

• PDFs

• Product manuals

• Internal company knowledge

• Research papers

• Customer support articles
A Large Language Model cannot automatically access these documents.
You need a way to:

• Convert documents into embeddings.

• Store those embeddings efficiently.

• Search for semantically similar content.

• Send the relevant context to the LLM.
This is exactly what Chroma helps you do.
What is Chroma?
Chroma is an open-source vector database designed for AI applications.
It allows developers to:

• Store embeddings

• Perform semantic search

• Retrieve relevant documents

• Build RAG applications

• Manage AI knowledge bases
Unlike traditional databases that search using exact keywords, Chroma searches using meaning and context.
For example:
User query:
How can I reset my account password?Stored document:
Steps to change your login credentialsA traditional database might not find a match.
Chroma can recognize that both texts have similar meaning and return the relevant document.
Understanding Embeddings
Before understanding Chroma, it’s important to understand embeddings.
Embeddings are numerical representations of text.
For example:
"I love JavaScript"might become:
[0.42, 0.81, -0.15, 0.67, ...]Similarly:
"I enjoy coding in JS"will produce a vector that is close in mathematical space.
Because similar meanings generate similar vectors, Chroma can efficiently find related content.
How Chroma Works
A typical workflow looks like this:
Step 1: Load Documents
documents = [
"JavaScript is a programming language.",
"Python is widely used in AI."
]Step 2: Generate Embeddings
An embedding model converts text into vectors.
embeddings = embedding_model.embed(documents)Step 3: Store in Chroma
collection.add(
documents=documents,
embeddings=embeddings
)Step 4: Query Chroma
User asks:
Tell me about JavaScriptChroma searches for semantically similar vectors and returns:
JavaScript is a programming language.The retrieved content can then be sent to an LLM as additional context.
Installing Chroma
Installation is straightforward.
pip install chromadbCreate a database:
import chromadbclient = chromadb.Client()
collection = client.create_collection(
name="documents"
)
You now have a local vector database ready to store embeddings.
Basic Example
Adding data:
collection.add(
ids=["1", "2"],
documents=[
"JavaScript is used for web development.",
"Python is popular in machine learning."
]
)Searching:
results = collection.query(
query_texts=["What language is used for websites?"],
n_results=1
)
print(results)Chroma returns the most relevant document based on semantic similarity.
Why Chroma is Popular
Developer-Friendly
Getting started requires only a few lines of code.
Open Source
Developers can run Chroma locally without licensing costs.
Built for AI
Unlike traditional databases, Chroma is specifically optimized for embedding storage and retrieval.
Fast Semantic Search
Chroma can efficiently search through thousands or millions of embeddings.
Easy Integration
Works well with:

• LangChain

• LlamaIndex

• OpenAI

• Anthropic

• Hugging Face

• Custom embedding models
Chroma in RAG Applications
One of the most common uses of Chroma is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).
The workflow looks like this:
User Question
↓
Generate Query Embedding
↓
Search Chroma
↓
Retrieve Relevant Documents
↓
Send Context to LLM
↓
Generate Accurate ResponseThis approach helps LLMs answer questions using external knowledge rather than relying solely on training data.
Use Cases
AI Chatbots
Provide answers from company-specific documentation.
Customer Support
Search support articles and FAQs semantically.
Enterprise Search
Allow employees to search internal knowledge bases.
Research Assistants
Retrieve relevant papers and references.
Document Q&A Systems
Enable users to ask questions about PDFs, reports, and manuals.
Chroma vs Traditional Databases
Traditional databases are excellent for:

• Exact matches

• Structured records

• Transactions

• Relational data
Chroma excels at:

• Semantic search

• Similarity matching

• Embedding storage

• AI-powered retrieval
Rather than replacing traditional databases, Chroma often works alongside them.
Limitations of Chroma
While powerful, Chroma isn’t the best solution for every scenario.
Consider alternatives when:

• You need complex relational queries.

• You require large-scale enterprise database features.

• You need transactional consistency similar to SQL databases.
For AI retrieval systems and RAG applications, however, Chroma is often an excellent choice.
Summary
Chroma is an open-source vector database built specifically for AI applications. It stores embeddings and enables semantic search, making it a core component of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems.
By allowing developers to retrieve relevant information based on meaning rather than exact keywords, Chroma helps Large Language Models access external knowledge and generate more accurate responses.
